instructions: The night before, or at least 8 hours ahead: put a dry skillet over medium heat. Add the 1 tbsp cumin seeds, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp fenugreek seeds, 5 cloves, the cinnamon, the 10 peppercorns, the seeds from the 4 cardamom pods and the 4 dried chilies. Toast them for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking the pan, until they smell fragrant and feel warm. Take them off before they smoke and tip them onto a plate to cool.

Grind the cooled spices to a fine powder in a spice grinder or blender. Peel and roughly chop 1 tbsp of the ginger and peel 4 of the garlic cloves. Add them to the blender with the 1/3 cup vinegar, 1 tbsp tamarind paste, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1/2 tsp turmeric and 1 tsp of the salt, and blend to a smooth paste.
Trim off any thick pieces of fat and cut the pork into 1 1/2 inch cubes. Toss them in a bowl with all of the paste until every piece is coated. Cover and refrigerate overnight.
On the day, take the pork out of the fridge about 30 minutes before you start. Meanwhile, cut the remaining 6 garlic cloves into thin slivers, finely chop the 2 onions and chop the 4 tomatoes.
Slice the 2 green chilies thinly and put them in a small bowl for the table. Cut the lime in half.

Heat the 1/4 cup oil in a Dutch oven or heavy pot over low heat. Add the garlic slivers and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until they're soft and pale gold. Watch them closely. Burnt garlic tastes bitter. Lift them out onto a plate with a slotted spoon.

Turn the heat to medium high. When the oil shimmers, add the 1 tsp mustard seeds. When they start to pop, after about 30 seconds, add 20 of the curry leaves and fry them for 15 seconds. Stand back a little. They'll spatter.
Add the onions with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and cook for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring, until they're soft and starting to turn golden.
Stir in the 2 tsp chili powder and cook for 30 seconds.
Add the pork and all of its marinade. Cook for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until the paste darkens and starts to stick to the bottom a little.

Add the tomatoes and 2 cups water and scrape up anything stuck to the bottom. Bring it to a boil, then cover, turn the heat to low and simmer gently for 60 to 75 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick. The pork is done when a cube breaks apart easily with a spoon.
If the sauce is still thin, take the lid off and simmer for 5 to 10 minutes, until it coats the pork.
Stir in about two thirds of the fried garlic and squeeze in the juice of one lime half. Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt or a squeeze of the other lime half.
Serve over basmati rice with the rest of the fried garlic on top and the sliced green chilies on the side.
advance_prep_notes: make the spice paste and marinate the pork overnight, the night before
method_notes: Every version grinds toasted whole spices and dried red chilies with garlic, ginger and vinegar into a paste, marinates pork shoulder in it, then simmers it with fried onion until the pork is tender. Great Curry Recipes adds tamarind, brown sugar and fenugreek to the paste, fries garlic slivers, mustard seeds and curry leaves before the onions and tomatoes, and finishes with lime. Hari Ghotra grinds onion into the paste, adds potatoes and marinates only 20 minutes; Kavey Eats fries the marinated pork until the paste browns before adding tomato, tamarind and jaggery. This one follows Great Curry Recipes, with the fry of the paste from Kavey Eats, mild Kashmiri chilies in the pot and the green chilies moved to the table.
